The first time I sat at a sushi counter in Tokyo, I made every mistake possible. I had read a guidebook on the plane, but I had forgotten most of it by the time I arrived. I was wearing a strong perfume, which is a bad idea, because the smell is too close to the fish. While the chef was preparing the first piece, I was taking photos with my phone. And when he put the sushi in front of me, I waited too long. A good chef wants you to eat each piece immediately, while the rice is still warm. He didn't say anything, of course. But my host told me later that the chef had been watching me all night, and that he had decided I was a good student, because I had asked so many questions.

I grew up in Bologna, in a family of cooks, so I thought I knew everything about fresh ingredients. Then, when I was twenty-six, I went to Osaka to work in a small restaurant for one year. On my first day, the chef gave me a knife and a bag of rice. For three months, I didn't touch any fish. I washed rice, I cleaned the counter, and I watched. I had been working there for almost six months when he finally let me prepare a simple dish. I was so nervous that my hands were shaking. Today I have my own restaurant in Milan, and the menu changes every season, like in Osaka. Italian and Japanese food are more similar than people think. Few ingredients, very fresh, and a lot of respect.

My first business dinner in Japan was fifteen years ago, and I still remember it. Our host had booked a private room, and there were twelve people at the table. Everything was going well until the drinks arrived. I was thirsty, so I filled my own glass with beer. Suddenly, the room went quiet. Nobody had told me that in Japan you don't pour your own drink. You pour for the people next to you, and they pour for you. My colleague, who had been living in Tokyo for years, quickly picked up the bottle and filled everybody's glass, and the conversation started again. Later, our host laughed about it and made a toast to our Dutch friend, who was learning fast.
